item.visible_content: Two figures, two pages apart, shot at the same waterfront location with the same two actors in the same wardrobe and the same framing scale. Figure 5.4 (correct) pairs three overhead diagrams with three frames: D a wide two-shot, E character A at frame left looking frame right, F character B right of centre looking frame LEFT. Figure 5.5 (incorrect) reuses frames D and E unchanged and replaces F with the same actor now placed at frame LEFT looking frame RIGHT. The third diagram in 5.5 carries the drawn label "WRONG SIDE OF LINE".
item.what_the_visual_supports: That crossing the action line for one shot of a dialogue pair makes both characters appear to look the same way, so they read as addressing an unseen third person. The pair holds location, talent, wardrobe, scale and shot A constant and changes only which side of the line the camera sat on for character B.
item.requires_prose: The naming of the line as the axis of action, the 180-degree arc it establishes, and the rule that all coverage must come from one side of it.
item.extractor_note: This is a genuine minimal pair — one variable changed, the rest held — and it is the strongest piece of evidence in the section. In the extracted text it is reduced to two nearly identical caption sentences and a scatter of the letters A through F. Nothing in the text indicates that 5.4 and 5.5 are the same setup photographed twice, which is the entire point.

item.label: continuity_geometry
item.basis: The chapter derives sight line, axis of action, the 180 degree arc, the 30 degree increment and the line-crossing failure from one another in an explicit chain, and treats them as one body of craft under the heading of continuity. The grouping is the source's organising move.

item.label: continuity_geometry_of_the_action_line
item.description: A single geometric construction generates most of this chapter's rules. Attention between subjects creates a sight line; tracing that sight line fixes the action line; the action line cuts the circle of possible camera positions into two halves; staying in one half preserves screen direction; crossing it reverses direction; and reciprocal coverage positions are computed by mirroring across the same line. The rules are consequences of one plan drawing, not a list.

whole_system_claim.text: Screen direction, the 180 degree rule, jumping the line, the 30 degree rule and reciprocating imagery are all derived from a single imaginary line established by the talent's own sight line. Once that line is fixed, the permitted camera positions, the mirrored positions for matched coverage and the failure mode of crossing it all follow geometrically.

source_ref.section: The Imaginary Line—The 180 Degree Rule; The 30 Degree Rule

dependencies.nature: the line is established by tracing a sight line
the arc is defined by the line

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: The derivation chain is the source's own: it states that the line is traced from the sight line, that the arc follows from the line, that the 30 degree slices sit within the arc, and that reciprocal setups mirror across it. What is ours is treating maintained screen direction as a property the system preserves rather than as a further member.

source_terms: By keeping the camera essentially in the same place, and moving the actors, you can capture all the motion and emotion of the scene without any complex moves.

item.claim: Technique 8.7. For an argument, hold a wide master with almost no camera movement and let the actors circle and pace, blocked so that whoever is dominating the scene faces the camera and the turn has already happened before the other begins to dominate. The source states the standing problem — one actor is always facing away — and requires that actor to be given enough body acting to keep a presence. It also gives a fallback: if no take is perfect, shoot coverage that need not be faces, since hands and feet will enable a cut while keeping the focus on the argument's energy.

mechanism.text: People arguing circle and pace, so the movement the scene needs is already there; making the actors carry it keeps the audience oriented in a way a moving camera would not.

scope.conditions: arguments and other scenes with continuous movement between two people

caveats.text: the only technique in the chapter that solves the chapter's problem without moving the camera at all, and the only one that ends by planning for a cut

item.question: What licensed spending in the household this source describes, and what was treated as the enemy?
item.answer: An occasion licensed spending; impulse was the enemy. He describes growing up in middle-class India as 'an elaborate exercise in learning to detach action from one's senses' — ice cream was not eaten because one felt like it but on occasions when celebrations had been planned, and new clothes were bought with ceremony at festivals. Festivals functioned as 'the safety valves in our otherwise restrained lives', supplying permission the individual's own appetite was not allowed to supply. The mechanism is that where budgets are tight and every deviation is felt as risk, the sense that prompts spending has to be disconnected from the act, and an external calendar then supplies the sanction.
item.support: 'Festivals were the safety valves in our otherwise restrained lives; they gave us sanction to experience little atolls of freedom.'
item.confounders: Wholly retrospective — an adult recalling a childhood household with no contemporaneous record — and the book's second section is explicitly about these constraints loosening.

item.rationale: SPEC-01 carries a dialogue_intent field. This source says something specific and unobvious about it: dialogue and sound effects compete for one pool of attention, so the amount of dialogue determines what the rest of the soundtrack can carry. Reducing dialogue is not merely removing words — it promotes everything else. Any specification of dialogue intent for a video creative is therefore also, implicitly, a specification of how much the rest of the sound can do.

applicability.when: specifying dialogue for a video creative whose soundtrack is doing narrative or emotional work
applicability.limits: The source's evidence is one film, and he states he was not conscious of the effect while making it and reconstructed it afterwards from audience reaction. The claim is a maker's retrospective account of his own work, which is a weaker evidential position than it reads as.

source_terms: M: That's the great power of source music—music that comes from within the scene
M: they are insulated from feeling overtly manipulated musically because the sounds are explained by the scene
M: It sneaks past their immune system, so to speak. Whereas a musical score doesn't. It has to pass through some sort of blood/brain barrier.
item.claim: Murch's account of why music originating inside a scene — an orchestra shown playing, a radio, a record player — works differently from a score. Because the scene explains the sound, the audience is insulated from feeling musically manipulated: it reads as an accident of the filming, not as commentary on the subtext, even though it is commentary. A score is perceived as a new voice entering, and the viewer repositions slightly on hearing it. Murch says sound effects work the same way, and that both aim at the ideal of the lucky accident.

mechanism.text: Attribution governs the defence. Sound the audience can attribute to the world of the scene is not experienced as authored, so it is not resisted. Sound with no in-world source is experienced as an authorial voice and triggers a slight repositioning.

scope.conditions: any music or effect whose origin can be located within a scene

caveats.text: Murch immediately reports playing against his own principle: in The English Patient a piece was set up to be heard as score and then revealed to be a record playing in the scene, which he says has "almost the opposite" effect to the one he has just described
he bounds it himself: "If you overuse it, then it becomes predictable and it's not so welcome anymore." Recorded as sk_conv_c003_0011.
the mechanism is an unexamined metaphor — an immune system, a blood/brain barrier. It is doing real explanatory work and it is not evidence.

source_terms: M: I think that encourages the audience to listen to sounds as if they are speech. In other words, you begin to search the soundtrack for meaning because there are no words "in the foreground" distracting you.
M: You pay attention to the stars on nights when there is no moon. When the moon is shining, all you can see is the moon. Dialogue is the moon, and stars are the sound effects.
item.claim: Murch's claim about attention across the soundtrack: dialogue and sound effects compete, and withdrawing dialogue causes the audience to search the remaining sound for meaning, listening to sounds as if they were speech. His figure is the moon and the stars — the stars are visible on nights when the moon is not shining. He notes the sound effects themselves did not change between the halves of the film; what changed was the gradual evaporation of dialogue.

mechanism.text: Attention is a fixed quantity competing across one channel. Words in the foreground consume it; remove them and the same effects, unchanged, acquire a significance they would not otherwise have.

scope.conditions: a soundtrack in which dialogue can be reduced

caveats.text: Murch states he did not do this knowingly: "Curiously, I wasn't consciously aware of this when I was working on the film." He worked it out only after audiences remarked on the soundtrack, and says "It seems obvious in retrospect."

that admission is the most epistemically interesting moment in the chapter. The claim is a post-hoc reconstruction of the maker's own work, offered by the maker, which is a weaker evidential position than it appears to be — and the source volunteers the weakness rather than concealing it.
the control the claim rests on is real and stated: the effects did not differ between the two halves, only the dialogue did

source_stated_remedies: withdraw dialogue to make the audience attend to the rest of the soundtrack

positive.description: the last half of The Conversation, in which dialogue gradually evaporates leaving the recorded conversation itself and the sound effects

intra_source_relations.note: sound perspective carrying the plot depends on the audience attending to sound

item.label: seven_ways_to_move_attention_without_a_cut
item.description: Chapter 8 read as a set of alternatives to cutting: motivate a move with an object in transit; hand the scene from one subject to another with a retreating camera; carry the move on an actor's differential speed across the lens; put subject and reaction in one frame with a reflection; drive the camera to a predetermined close-up regardless of the action; identify a background figure by an established colour; or move nobody but the actors in a static wide master.

whole_system_claim.text: The seven are alternative answers to one question — how to redirect attention without a cut — and they differ in what carries the redirection: an object, the camera's retreat, an actor's speed, a reflective surface, the camera's indifference, a colour, or blocking. Two of the seven use no camera movement at all, which is why the set is better described by what redirects attention than by what the camera does.
whole_system_claim.interpretation_basis: The source never states a chapter thesis; each technique stands alone under its own number. The reading is ours, and its basis is that six of the seven explicitly contrast their method with cutting or with a plain pan, and the chapter is the author's own grouping under the title Directing Attention. The parameter that distinguishes the members — what carries the redirection — is also ours.

tradeoffs.nature: Both depend on a lens decision that determines what the background does, and they pull opposite ways. The reflection technique warns that a long lens leaves the reflection blurred unless focus is pulled; the colour technique wants a long lens precisely so the background blurs. The same choice serves one and damages the other.

conflicts.nature: The chapter's last technique reaches the chapter's goal without moving the camera at all, and ends by planning coverage so that a cut becomes possible. Whatever unifies these seven techniques, it is not the avoidance of cutting as such.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Membership and order are the source's — these are its seven numbered techniques under its own chapter title. Everything else here is ours: the framing claim, the parameter that separates the members, the recorded trade-off between two lens decisions, and the observation that the final technique breaks the pattern. A reader could take the chapter as an unordered list of seven unrelated tricks, and nothing in the source contradicts that.
